description:

A useful first test is to choose a small set of icons and see how they look in the actual website or application before downloading a large collection.

Choose the asset type for the job

An icon is most useful when it helps someone recognize an action or section. A detailed illustration can explain a service or support an empty screen. A 3D asset can give a campaign a distinctive look. A short animation can show a change in status or draw attention to a result. Use the simplest asset that communicates what the viewer needs to know.

If you are building a navigation menu, the icons should make it easier to scan the labels. If you are preparing a landing page, a larger illustration may help explain the offer. Treat the text and visual as a pair. An unfamiliar icon used alone can be hard to understand, even if it looks attractive in the library. Test it in context with the actual label, button or message.

Build an icon set around a real interface

Imagine a freelance developer is building a client dashboard for a training company. The main sections are lessons, progress, downloads and account settings. Choose one visual style for those sections and look for icons that share the same line weight, corner shape and level of detail. Place them next to the real labels. A compact menu works best when each icon remains recognizable at the size used on the page.

Check whether the set contains enough related icons for future additions. You might need notifications, help and billing later. A set that fits the first four menu items may be harder to extend if related actions use a different visual style. Keep a record of the asset collection and the exact icon names so another developer can find matching files.

Inspect the files at the final size

Open the icon in the format you plan to use. A vector file can remain clear at different sizes, but its artwork still needs enough space between important shapes. Small details may disappear in a sixteen-pixel placement. Test the icon on both light and dark backgrounds if your application supports them. Choose colors with enough contrast for the action to remain clear.

When the asset is used with a visible label, the label should explain the action. An icon-only control needs an accessible name, and a decorative icon can be handled separately so it does not repeat the visible text for someone using a screen reader. Test the final interface with keyboard navigation and review whether the icon communicates enough in each state.

Create a consistent illustration system

Illustrations can add context to a website or application. For the dashboard example, an empty download section might show a simple folder illustration and explain when course files will appear. A progress page might use a more detailed graphic to introduce the learning report. Both can share colors and shapes while serving different purposes.

Choose a small set of colors and a consistent level of detail. Look for illustrations that use similar proportions and line treatment. Place the graphics next to the real headings and check whether they support the message. Avoid using a large illustration if it pushes important instructions below the visible part of a mobile screen. The page should remain understandable when the visual is removed or slow to load.

Recolor with a limited palette

Start with the main colors used by the website or app. Recolor the asset only where the supplied file and terms allow it. Keep neutral tones where they improve readability. For example, a blue highlight can match the interface while light gray and white separate the details. Check the result against both the brand reference and the existing page backgrounds.

Save the edited and original files separately. Record the color choices and intended placement so you can produce future assets that fit the same system. If an editor allows you to apply a palette to several assets, inspect each output for details that became hard to distinguish. A consistent palette is useful only when the icons and illustrations remain legible.

Choose 3D assets for a clear purpose

A 3D illustration can add depth to a landing page or help establish a visual theme. Compare the angle, lighting and shape with the other elements in the design. A collection of assets that use similar lighting can look more coherent than individual objects chosen from unrelated sources. If your team needs to edit or render the object, confirm the file format and compatibility before choosing it.

Use one strong object as the main visual when the surrounding text is important. A busy group of objects can compete with a headline or call to action. Test the composition on a mobile screen and check the rendered image size for a website. Keep the editable source when you are allowed to retain it and prepare a smaller export suited to the placement.

Use Lottie animation to explain a change

A short animation can help someone understand when an upload is complete or show a transition between steps. Decide which state the animation communicates. A completion animation should play after the task has finished. A loading visual should make it clear that the system is still working. Use text where the information matters so the animation is not the only way the viewer can learn what happened.

Check the format and the requirements of your website or application. Test the animation in the real player. The preview in an asset library may not reflect the dimensions, background or rendering behavior of your implementation. Review the loop, speed and color. Consider a static version for situations where motion is reduced or unnecessary.

Keep animation light and readable

A small motion detail can help draw attention to an important part of the page. Too much movement can distract from the task, especially on a screen with several controls. Test the page in normal use and watch how long the animation runs. Choose a short sequence that supports the interface without interrupting the next action.

Check the file size and the effect on page performance. An animation may be useful on an onboarding screen, while a simple static icon can be enough for a repeated navigation item. Keep both versions if you need a fallback. Record the intended behavior with the asset so a developer knows whether it should play once, loop or respond to a specific event.

Organize source files and licensing records

Record the asset link, chosen format and applicable terms when you add a resource to a project. A client may ask where an icon came from or whether it can be reused in another campaign. Keeping that record makes it easier to answer. Review whether the terms allow your intended use and sharing of raw files. A finished website or presentation can have different needs from a downloadable asset pack.

Prepare a small handover folder. Include the files needed for the approved implementation and a short note about where each is used. Keep editable sources separate from production exports. When possible, name files by purpose, such as lesson progress icon or completion animation, so the next person can find them without opening each file.

Compare IconScout with related design tools

For broader vector and stock-photo selection, review Vecteezy or Freepik. For precise editing of vector shapes and text, compare Adobe Creative Cloud. Check how the files move from the resource library to the tool you use for final delivery.

For simple layouts, explore Canva. If you need video-oriented motion templates, see Motion Array. If the project needs new visual concepts before you choose supporting icons, review Leonardo AI. Compare the resources based on the work you need to deliver and the control you need over the finished files.

Decide whether IconScout fits your budget

List the projects that need visual resources during the access period. Count the distinct icons, illustrations or motion assets you need and test a small sample in the actual site or application. Consider the time it takes to find a matching set, adjust the colors and prepare the correct format. A smaller set that fits the project can be more valuable than a large download collection.

If you have a team, agree on which collections and styles will be reused. Test the files in the tools that each person uses and document the process. A designer may need editable assets, while a developer needs compact production files. Make sure the resource supports both roles before applying it across a large project.

Frequently asked questions

What should I look for in an icon set?

Look for consistent shapes, spacing and line weight. Check that the collection covers the actions you need and that the icons remain clear at the smallest planned size. Place them next to the real labels and test the interface in both light and dark settings if needed. Keep the collection reference with the project for future additions.

Can I edit the asset colors?

Check the available file format and editing tools for the asset. Some formats allow more control than others. Confirm that the usage terms cover the changes you need. Compare the result on the real background, and keep the original alongside the edited copy so you can revisit the choice later.

Can I use the animations on a website?

Check the file format and make sure it works with your website’s player or implementation. Test the animation in the target placement and review performance on a mobile device. Prepare a clear static or text version if the animation communicates an important status. Review the applicable license for the intended use.

How do I check the current access offer?

Use the IconScout order page to review current subscription options and checkout price. Contact 24/7 Live Chat Support for help with access. Pick one real project to test the resources and formats before depending on a particular asset for a deadline.

IconScout group buy is most useful when your project calls for consistent icons, illustrations or motion details. Choose assets that support a real interface or campaign, test them in place and keep their source records. Browse the SEOGBTools shop for complementary design tools if you also need to edit and export the finished work.

Check an icon family before the handover

Make a small reference page with the icons at their normal sizes. Place each one next to its real label and include the default, active and disabled colors if the interface uses them. Look for icons that are too similar when viewed side by side. For example, two folder shapes may be difficult to tell apart if they stand for lessons and downloads. Keep the labels clear and change the icon that communicates the weaker distinction.

Add a note about the file format and intended size to the project handover. If your developer needs to recolor the icon in the application, test the file in the same component that will use it. For a marketing page, check whether the final export still looks sharp after the site compresses it. Keep the source and the web version together.
